'''''Eucalyptus crebra''''', commonly known as the '''narrow-leaved ironbark''', '''narrow-leaved red ironbark''' or simply '''ironbark''',<ref name="CANBR">{{cite web |title=''Eucalyptus crebra'' |url=https://apps.lucidcentral.org/euclid/text/entities/eucalyptus_crebra.htm |publisher=Euclid: Centre for Australian National Biodiversity Research |access-date=4 June 2020}}</ref> and as '''muggago''' in the indigenous [[Tharawal|Dharawal]] language,<ref name=RBGS>{{cite web|url=http://plantnet.rbgsyd.nsw.gov.au/cgi-bin/NSWfl.pl?page=nswfl&lvl=sp&name=Eucalyptus~crebra|title=''Eucalyptus crebra'' F.Muell.|last=Hill|first=Ken|date=1999|work=PlantNet - New South Wales Flora Online|publisher= Royal Botanic Gardens & Domain Trust, Sydney Australia|access-date=2009-06-21}}</ref> is a species of small to medium-sized tree [[Endemism|endemic]] to eastern [[Australia]]. It has hard, rough "[[ironbark]]" from its trunk to small branches, linear to lance-shaped adult leaves, flower buds in groups of seven, nine or eleven, white flowers and cup-shaped, barrel-shaped or hemispherical fruit. A variable species, it grows in woodland and forest from the [[Cape York Peninsula]] to near [[Sydney]]. It is an important source of nectar in the honey industry and its hard, strong timber is used in construction.[[File:Eucalyptus crebra buds.jpg|thumb|Flower buds]][[File:Eucalyptus crebra fruit.jpg|thumb|Fruit]][[File:Eucalyptus crebra tree.jpg|thumb|Habit in coastal Central Queensland.]]

==Description==
''Eucalyptus crebra'' is a tree that typically grows to a height of {{cvt|35|m}} and forms a [[lignotuber]]. It has persistent thick, rough, deeply furrowed, greyish black "ironbark" from the base of its trunk to the small branches. Young plants and [[coppice]] regrowth have linear to lance-shaped or curved leaves {{cvt|50-120|mm}} long and {{cvt|6-17|mm}} wide. Adult leaves are linear to lance-shaped, the same dull green to greyish colour on both sides, {{cvt|55-180|mm}} long and {{cvt|7-27|mm}} wide on a [[Petiole (botany)|petiole]] {{cvt|7-20|mm}} long. The flower buds are arranged in groups of seven, nine or eleven, usually on a branching [[inflorescence]] on the ends of branchlets. Each group is carried on a [[Peduncle (botany)|peduncle]] {{cvt|2-13|mm}} long, the individual buds on a [[Pedicel (botany)|pedicel]] {{cvt|2-7|mm}} long. Mature buds are club-shaped, spindle-shaped, or diamond-shaped to oval, {{cvt|3-7|mm}} long and {{cvt|2-4|mm}} wide and green to yellow with a conical to rounded [[Operculum (botany)|operculum]]. Flowering has been recorded in most months and the flowers are white. The fruit is a woody cup-shaped, barrel-shaped or hemispherical [[Capsule (botany)|capsule]] {{cvt|2-7|mm}} long and {{cvt|2.5-6|mm}} wide on a pedicel {{cvt|1-6|mm}} long.<ref name="CANBR" /><ref name="RBGS" /><ref name="ABRS">{{cite web |last1=Chippendale |first1=George M. |title=''Eucalyptus crebra'' |url=https://profiles.ala.org.au/opus/foa/profile/Eucalyptus%20crebra |publisher=Australian Biological Resources Study, Department of the Environment and Energy, Canberra |access-date=17 May 2019}}</ref>

==Taxonomy and naming==
''Eucalyptus crebra'' was first formally described in ''Journal and Proceedings of the Linnean Society, Botany'' by [[Victoria (Australia)|Victorian]] state botanist [[Ferdinand von Mueller]] in 1859.<ref name=APNI>{{cite web|title=''Eucalyptus crebra''|url= https://id.biodiversity.org.au/instance/apni/456095|publisher=APNI|access-date=16 May 2019}}</ref><ref name="F.Muell.">{{cite journal |last1=von Mueller |first1=Ferdinand |title=Monograph of the Eucalypti of tropical Australia |journal=Journal of the Proceedings of the Linnean Society, Botany |date=1859 |volume=3 |page=87 |url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/8353#page/91/mode/1up |access-date=17 May 2019}}</ref> The [[Botanical name|specific epithet]] is the [[Latin]] adjective ''crebra'' meaning "thick", "close" or "numerous",<ref name="RWB">{{cite book|last1=Brown|author-link1=Roland W. Brown|first1=Roland Wilbur|title=The Composition of Scientific Words|date=1956|publisher=Smithsonian Institution Press|location=Washington, D.C.|page=790}}</ref><ref name=EJ>{{cite encyclopedia |author1=Elliot, Rodger W.  |author2=Jones, David L. | year = 1986 | title = Eu-Go | editor = Elliot, Rodger W. |editor2=Jones, David L. | encyclopedia = Encyclopaedia of Australian Plants suitable for cultivation | volume = 4 | pages = 66–67 | publisher = Lothian Publishing | isbn = 0-85091-213-X}}</ref> referring to the species' abundance.<ref name="CANBR" />

Narrow-leaved ironbark has included several species, including ''E. drepanophylla'' and ''E. xanthoclada'' but these are regarded as [[Taxonomic synonym|synonyms]] by the [[Australian Plant Census]]. ''Eucalyptus repanophylla'' is accepted as a separate species by the Queensland Government.<ref name="APC" /><ref name="QLD">{{cite web |title=''Eucalyptus drepanophylla'' |date=20 October 2014 |url=https://wetlandinfo.des.qld.gov.au/wetlands/ecology/components/species/?eucalyptus-drepanophylla |publisher=Queensland Government department of Environment and Science |access-date=17 May 2019}}</ref> Other similar species include ''[[Eucalyptus exilipes|E. exilipes]]'', ''[[Eucalyptus granitica|E. granitica]]'', ''[[Eucalyptus staigeriana|E. staigeriana]]'', ''[[Eucalyptus quadricostata|E. quadricostata]]'' and ''[[Eucalyptus whitei|E. whitei]]''.<ref name="CANBR" />

==Distribution and habitat==
The narrow-leaved ironbark grows in sandy soils in woodland and forest from [[Picton, New South Wales|Picton]], southwest of Sydney, north through New South Wales and Queensland to the vicinity of [[Moreton Telegraph Station]] on [[Cape York Peninsula]].<ref name="CANBR" /><ref name="RBGS" /><ref name=EJ/>

==Uses==
The tree has a hard, strong, and dark red timber, which has been used for [[Railroad tie|sleepers]] and construction.<ref name=EJ/> A plank has been recorded as being used for [[Elizabeth Farm, New South Wales|Elizabeth Farm]], Australia's oldest surviving European dwelling.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.dhub.org/object/224294,swann|title=D6911 Timber specimen (plank), Ironbark (Eucalyptus crebra), used in the building of stables at Elizabeth Farm, Rose Hill, New South Wales, Australia, 1793|author=D'Hub (Design Hub)|work=D'hub - Your online design resource|publisher=Powerhouse Museum, Sydney|access-date=2009-06-24}}{{Dead link|date=August 2019 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}</ref> It is used as a shade tree or to line roadways, and is also available as a cultivar. It is useful in honey production as the flowers are heavy in nectar and pollen;<ref name=EJ/> the resulting honey produced by bees is light-coloured and delicately flavoured.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.capilano.com.au/education/floral-varieties.aspx |title=Floral Varieties |author=Capilano Honey |date=2006 |work=Capilano Honey |access-date=2009-06-24 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090505110621/http://www.capilano.com.au/education/floral-varieties.aspx |archive-date=May 5, 2009 }}</ref>
